evidence: The surviving solution explicitly begins with "# bipartition via BFS" and constructs colors for every component.
affordance_in_statement: The system architecture strictly divides all microservices into exactly two underlying camps. ... The analyzer guarantees that every conflict pair consists of one microservice from the first camp and one from the second camp. There are never any conflicts between two microservices that belong to the same camp.
removal_suggestion: Remove the explicit promise that every conflict crosses two camps, or re-present the input as an arbitrary conflict graph that may contain odd cycles and same-camp conflicts. This prevents bipartition-side selection, though it changes the underlying problem to general independent-set selection.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Uses the guaranteed bipartite structure, BFS-colors each connected component, and selects independent color classes rather than solving arbitrary independent set.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The analyzer guarantees that every conflict pair consists of one microservice from the first camp and one from the second camp.

common_affordance: the guaranteed two-camp (bipartite conflict graph) structure

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: Its BFS-based implementation mishandles the component-wise bipartition/selection logic, so it does not reliably construct a sufficiently large independent set even though the graph is bipartite.
Its coloring-based approach does not correctly handle the required component-wise choice and reconstruction of the selected vertices.
Its BFS coloring/selection implementation is incomplete or incorrect for the required independent-set output, despite relying on the bipartite promise.

recommended_edit: Delete the explicit two-camp guarantee and state that conflict pairs form an arbitrary undirected conflict graph, potentially containing odd cycles and conflicts within either camp.
regression_risk: This may restore the already-defeated models if their implementations happen to produce valid answers on the new test cases, and it also substantially changes the problem's computational difficulty.
